# VetReception

> The phone answered every time, triaged to the practice's own protocol, booked into the PIMS.

VetReception answers every call a veterinary practice cannot get to — after hours, during surgery, and at three in the morning — triages it against the practice's own emergency protocol rather than a generic script, books the appointment straight into the PIMS, and leaves the front desk a written summary instead of a voicemail to work through.

## Start here

- [VetReception: 24/7 Vet Call Answering Into Your PIMS](https://vetreception.swades.ai/): VetReception answers every veterinary call, triages against the practice's own written emergency protocol, and books straight into the PIMS.

## Veterinary Practices Pricing: How VetReception Is Priced
https://vetreception.swades.ai/pricing-for-veterinary-practices/

VetReception is priced per practice, not per call and not per minute. The number is set by how many phone lines ring into the practice, how many veterinarians are on the roster, and which PIMS the booking has to be written into — because each of those changes how much configuration and testing happens before the first call is answered.

The requirement is not a message service — it is a call that gets answered, triaged against the practice's own written emergency protocol, and booked into the PIMS before the caller hangs up.

## Vet Clinic Missed Calls: What They Cost and How to Stop Them
https://vetreception.swades.ai/the-problem-in-the-words-veterinary-practices-use/

A missed call at a small-animal practice is rarely a phone nobody heard. It is a call that arrived while the two people at the front desk were checking in a euthanasia, taking payment for a dental, and answering the other line. It is a call at 7:40pm after the last appointment, and a call at 3:12am from an owner whose dog is vomiting.

## VetReception Integrations: PIMS Booking and Call Summaries
https://vetreception.swades.ai/works-with-the-software-veterinary-practices-already-run/

An integration is the difference between a call that was answered and an appointment that exists. VetReception answers the calls your front desk cannot get to, and the connection is what turns that answered call into a booking written into the PIMS as a real appointment on the real schedule, with the client and patient matched to existing records where they exist.

## Vetspire Integration: 24/7 Vet Call Answering and Booking
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/vetspire-integration/

VetReception connects to Vetspire so that calls your front desk cannot reach are answered, triaged and booked without a human at the phone. The connection is a booking and record-writing integration, not a clinical one: the system reads your appointment types and provider availability from Vetspire and writes a booked appointment back into the same schedule your team already works from.

## Prescription Refill Request Line: 24/7 Vet Call Handling
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/prescription-refill-request-line/

A prescription refill request line is the number a client calls to ask for more of a medication their pet already takes. In most veterinary practices it is not a separate line at all — it is the same number clients use for appointments, emergencies and billing, and refill requests are one of the call types that arrive on it.

## Vet Clinic Missed Calls: What Happens and How to Stop Them
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/vet-clinic-missed-calls/

A missed call at a veterinary practice is not a message waiting to be returned. It is a client who dialled, heard nothing useful, and started looking for another number. The reason it happens is structural: the front desk is a single point of failure, and it is also the person checking in a vomiting dog, taking payment, and answering the line that is ringing right now.

## Veterinary Triage Protocol Phone: How Calls Get Sorted 24/7
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/veterinary-triage-protocol-phone/

A veterinary triage protocol phone answers every call a practice cannot get to, sorts it against the practice's own written emergency protocol, and writes the booking into the PIMS. The sorting rule is the practice's, not a generic urgency model, so the same symptom is handled the same way at 3am as it would be at 10am by the person who wrote the protocol.

## VetReception: What Happened at One Veterinary Practice
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/what-happened-at-one-of-our-veterinary-practices/

A three-veterinarian small-animal practice in the US had a PIMS, no overnight front desk, and a phone that went to voicemail between 6pm and 8am. After switching its after-hours line to VetReception, every call was answered, triaged against **the practice's own written emergency protocol**, and booked straight into the PIMS. The front desk arrived each morning to written summaries rather than a queue of voicemails.

## Emergency Vet Call Triage: How Calls Get Sorted 24/7
https://vetreception.swades.ai/blog/emergency-vet-call-triage/

Emergency vet call triage is the process of deciding, on the call itself, whether the animal needs to be seen now, today, or at a booked appointment — and then acting on that decision before the caller hangs up. VetReception does this against the practice's own written emergency protocol rather than a generic urgency model, and writes the outcome into the PIMS.

## Veterinary Practice Phone Terms: A Working Glossary
https://vetreception.swades.ai/the-terms-veterinary-practices-use/

Most veterinary call answering products are sold with the same six words — answer, triage, book, integrate, summarise, escalate — and mean different things by each. Two vendors can both claim "triage" while one applies a generic urgency model and the other reads the practice's own written emergency protocol. Getting the definitions straight first is what makes a demo comparable, and it is what makes a quote comparable.

## Veterinary Practices Use VetReception: Calls, Triage, PIMS
https://vetreception.swades.ai/how-veterinary-practices-use-it/

The calls that hurt are not the routine ones. They are the ones that arrive while the veterinarian is in surgery, while the front desk is checking in a euthanasia, or at 3am when nobody is in the building. A practice running one to six veterinarians with a PIMS and no overnight front desk has no third option: the phone rings out, the caller dials the next clinic, and the record of that call is a voicemail nobody has time to work through the next morning.
